title: The City of Bees
craft_focus: figurative comparison: the writer compares the hive to a city to explain it

source.basis: Adapted from Maurice Maeterlinck, The Life of the Bee (1901), translated by Alfred Sutro, under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Maeterlinck, Maurice. The Life of the Bee. Translated by Alfred Sutro. 1901. Project Gutenberg eBook #4511, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4511, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: Extracted a single 345-word passage; the authoring pass will split long sentences and drop rare words; no facts added.
source.survey: A worker bee shapes the first flake of wax and fixes it at the top of the dome, and the writer calls the hanging comb an inverted city.

license_evidence: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4511 lists the work under 'Copyright: Public domain in the USA.' and names Maeterlinck as author and Alfred Sutro as translator; the edition is the 1901 English translation, published in book form in 1901, so it is public domain in the United States.
notes: Anchor: 'for we have here an inverted city, hanging down from the sky, and not rising from the bosom of earth like a city of men' (paragraph 2, final sentence). A second simile, 'with the skill of a carpenter handling a pliable panel', sits two sentences earlier and supports the same craft point. Risks: the passage opens mid-explanation, so the adapted version must keep the first paragraph's fact that wax scales form on the bees' bodies; 'inverted cone', 'ivory tablets' and 'cupola' are archaic and need plain words, not new facts; 'alchemy' should become a plain phrase.
